newsitem.title: UK: UK'S SIB SETS TOUGH RULES FOR FUNDS AFTER DMG SAGA.
newsitem.headline: UK'S SIB SETS TOUGH RULES FOR FUNDS AFTER DMG SAGA.

text.p: Britain's top financial watchdog proposed on Wednesday changes to rules governing unit trusts and open ended investment companies after irregularities at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, which led to the dismissal of Morgan Grenfell Asset Managment fund manager Peter Young last September.
SIB said it proposed that in future, the total invested in pre-listed and unapproved securities should not exceed 10 percent of the value of the fund.

At present, funds can invest no more than 10 percent of their value in unlisted securities. However, there is no limit set on how much a fund can invest in pre-listed securities -- in other words, those which are not currently listed but are due to be within 12 months of their issue.
Under the new proposals, fund managers would also be required to make sure that overall the scheme shows a prudent spread of risks.
The SIB also proposed that unit trusts and open ended investment companies should be allowed to use the word guaranteed in their name, providing the fund meets certain standards.
The fund would have to obtain a legally enforceable guarantee, with the guarantor being subject to prudential supervision.
The standards also look at the nature of the guarantee and whether it is legally enforceable as well as the standing of the guarantor.

The SIB also said it was proposing to allow single pricing for unit trusts. At present, unit trusts are bought and sold on a dual price system, whereby the price at which they may be bought is higher than the sale price.
In the case of open ended investment companies, there is one price only based on net asset value.
